final.title: Requirement freeze works until the workflow changes
final.body:
If you run a small business, requirement freeze is worth rethinking in one narrow place: the workflow that changed after you wrote it down. That is usually where the friction shows up first. A repeat task starts needing exceptions, but the SOP or automation still assumes the old rule. Then the choice is not “AI or no AI.” It is more ordinary than that: keep the frozen spec and handle exceptions manually, update the spec and rebuild the workflow, or design the process to flag exceptions for human review. That third option is a design choice to be scoped in a diagnostic, not a claim that the system can decide for itself.

Bareni’s diagnostic approach fits this kind of decision: identify one recurring workflow, be honest about whether AI fits, and define scope and measures before anything is built. For a founder, the useful threshold is not a magic number. It is the point where exceptions are no longer rare enough to ignore. If you are spending more time on exceptions, the frozen requirement is no longer protecting you; it is hiding the gap between the process on paper and the process in real life.

A practical next step is simple: pick one documented workflow and ask, “What has changed since we froze this, and how many exceptions did I make this week?” If the answer is “too many to count,” the spec may be frozen in the wrong place. Human approval still owns any scope change, especially where money or other high-risk decisions are involved.
